summary: This was the weekly POC sync between Redwood (AE + SE) and BrightPath Health. Main topics: integration of Redwood SDK for function/tool calls, structured output schema implementation, observed parsing failures in 12% of cases, discussion of latency/cost tradeoffs and potential Dedicated capacity if throughput requirements persist. Action items assigned for SDK examples, integration test runs, and compliance questions. Next call: 2026-03-25 tentative.

1) SDK function/tool calling patterns and examples
2) Structured output (JSON schema) failures and mitigation
3) Latency profiling and batching strategies

transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Morning everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick roll call?
[00:05] Aisha Khan: Aisha here.
[00:07] Tom Reyes: Tom, hey.
[00:08] Priya Mehta: Priya.
[00:10] Liam O'Connor: Liam from Redwood, hi all.
[00:12] Jorge Alvarez: Jorge - security.
[00:15] Maya Chen: Great. Agenda — quick results review from last week's test, dig into the SDK tool/function calls, then structured output parsing issues, and action items.
[01:02] Tom Reyes: Quick note — we ran the 1k sample against the beta model last night, about 12% of responses failed to parse into our structured schema, mostly missing required fields or extra trailing text.
[01:25] Liam O'Connor: Okay can you share one of the failing payloads in the sheet? (laughter) — just kidding — but please paste. Typical causes are prompt ambiguity or model stopping early. Did you use the SDK call that returns the raw stream or the structured-output API?
[01:45] Tom Reyes: We used the SDK's chat completion with a function_call pattern, and then we tried to parse the assistant message into our JSON schema. We also added a stop token but not consistently.
[02:10] Priya Mehta: Some of the failures were like the assistant appending human-friendly commentary after the JSON blob, e.g., the JSON then a newline then 'Also, FYI...'.
[02:30] Maya Chen: Yep that's common. Two quick mitigations: 1) enforce structured output via the SDK's schema enforcement (we've added an example we can share), 2) post-validate and re-call with a validator prompt if parse fails. We'll share the sample snippet.
[03:00] Jorge Alvarez: From a security standpoint we want to ensure the logs don't contain PHI. Are we sending full transcript logs to Redwood?
[03:15] Maya Chen: For the hosted POC we only send request/response pairs. We can enable redaction and retention controls; for Dedicated or Private you can keep logs on-prem. We'll send the security doc link.
[03:40] Jorge Alvarez: Please also confirm KMS usage for model inputs/outputs at rest.
[03:52] Liam O'Connor: We support customer-managed KMS in Private and Dedicated. For hosted we offer envelope encryption and can integrate external KMS via our enterprise plan. I'll flag that in the notes.
[04:20] Tom Reyes: Back to parsing — Liam, you mentioned a schema enforcement, does that live client-side or server-side?
[04:32] Liam O'Connor: It's a mix. The SDK exposes a structured_output helper that triggers model-guided serialization server-side and also returns a parse-status field. If parse_status != OK you'll get raw_text for diagnostics. We recommend the client validate and then request a repair completion using the original context + validator prompt.
[05:05] Priya Mehta: Would that double our token cost?
[05:12] Maya Chen: Slightly, yes. Tradeoff is fewer developer hours spent on brittle regex parsers. We can show cost delta from our Optimize tool — small for low failure rates, but if you see 12% failures it adds up.
[05:40] Tom Reyes: The 12% was with our current prompts; after we tightened the instructions it dropped to about 6% in a smaller run.
[06:00] Liam O'Connor: Good. Also consider structured_output + strict_stop tokens; but watch out, strict stops can truncate if the model emits early. There's a balance.
[06:30] Maya Chen: On tool/function calling — are you calling internal services via Redwood's tool interface or mapping to local microservices?
[06:45] Tom Reyes: We map to internal microservices. We tried the example where the assistant returns an object with tool name and args then the client invokes the tool, but we had ordering issues when multiple calls were returned.
[07:05] Liam O'Connor: You likely received an array of actions. The SDK can normalize to a sequence and has a helper to run blocking calls vs async. If you need strict ordering, use the sequence mode and disable parallelization.
[07:40] Tom Reyes: Is that available in the JS and Python SDKs? We use Node.
[07:46] Liam O'Connor: Yes Node and Python both. I'll paste the Node snippet after the call.
[08:00] Priya Mehta: Any sample repos?
[08:04] Maya Chen: Yup, we'll share a small demo repo with the function calling flow wired to mock microservices. Link will be in the follow-up.
[08:20] Tom Reyes: Great. On latency — when we ran 200 concurrent requests the p95 shot to ~1.2s per token which is a bit high for our UI. We need <800ms p95.
[08:38] Liam O'Connor: Was that against hosted or Dedicated?
[08:41] Tom Reyes: Hosted.
[08:43] Liam O'Connor: For high concurrency, Dedicated or reserved capacity will give more predictable p95. Also batching helps reduce token cost but can increase tail latency in some scenarios. We can run a latency profile with your sample workload.
[09:05] Maya Chen: We can also recommend model quantization or a model variant with lower latency if quality tradeoff is acceptable.
[09:18] Priya Mehta: Quality can't dip below X threshold — our acceptance tests assert entity extraction accuracy.
[09:25] Maya Chen: Understood. We can tie the rollout to your eval run.
[09:35] Tom Reyes: A small technical question — when we call the SDK function_call with tools configured, how are credentials passed to the actual tool endpoints? Are they proxied through Redwood?
[09:49] Liam O'Connor: The SDK returns a tool-call payload; it's up to your client to invoke your endpoint. We don't proxy customer internal services in the hosted flow. For Private/Dedicated there is an option for secure connectors. We'll document the exact flow.
[10:08] Jorge Alvarez: For connectors, what's the authentication pattern? mTLS?
[10:15] Liam O'Connor: We support mTLS and token-based connectors depending on deployment. Private supports VPC peering and on-prem connectors.
[10:30] Maya Chen: Quick checkpoint — Liam will send the Node SDK snippet, Maya will share demo repo and structured-output example, Tom to run the larger integration test.
[11:00] Tom Reyes: One more wrinkle — sometimes the function args include free text that contains JSON inside strings, which our parser then double-parses and breaks. Any recommendations?
[11:12] Liam O'Connor: Best practice: encode nested JSON as base64 or as a string field and then decode client-side, or use an escaped JSON schema and strict validators. We'll include examples.
[11:35] Priya Mehta: Can the SDK automatically escape for us?
[11:39] Liam O'Connor: Not by default; it's safer to control it client-side, but we can add a wrapper in the demo repo.
[12:00] Maya Chen: Let's talk about monitoring — do you have visibility into model-level regressions?
[12:08] Tom Reyes: We collect metrics but need per-route breakdowns and sample-level traces to debug failures.
[12:16] Maya Chen: Redwood Console can show per-route token counts, latency distribution, and sample output traces. We can add your route and share a short walkthrough.
[12:30] Tom Reyes: That would help. Also want to correlate failed parses with tokens and chosen model.
[12:38] Liam O'Connor: Yup, Console traces include model variant and full response; you can filter by parse_status.
[12:50] Jorge Alvarez: Regarding compliance, do you have SOC 2 docs? Also we need retention options for logs — 30/90/365 days.
[12:58] Maya Chen: We have SOC 2 Type II and ISO docs; retention is configurable on Dedicated/Private and on hosted we offer configurable retention tiers. I'll share the security pack.
[13:20] Priya Mehta: Cost — if we add a repair call for parse failures at 6% expected, how much does that add?
[13:28] Maya Chen: Rough back-of-envelope: 6% extra calls * average tokens per repair (say 50 tokens) — we'll send a small cost estimate using your sample sheet. The Optimize tool can run that simulation.
[13:50] Tom Reyes: Ok thanks. For the POC acceptance criteria — we need <5% parse failures and p95 latency <800ms for the route. If both met we move to Dedicated evaluation.
[14:10] Maya Chen: Sounds good, we'll treat that as the gating criteria.
[14:20] Liam O'Connor: Short demo now — I'll share my screen to show sample Node flow (audio describes code).
[14:40] Speaker 2: [screen share but audio transcription noisy] "...use redwood.sdk.assistant.create..."
[15:05] Liam O'Connor: The key is setting function_call: 'auto' or explicit and structured_output: {schema: ...}. See line 34 in snippet.
[15:30] Tom Reyes: In your sample you allow multiple tool outputs, can we force only first match?
[15:36] Liam O'Connor: Yes, set max_tools:1 and sequence_mode: 'serial'.
[15:55] Priya Mehta: Any pitfalls for streaming vs non-streaming responses for structured output?
[16:04] Liam O'Connor: Streaming is great for UX but harder to guarantee strict JSON until end-of-stream; for strict schema enforcement non-streaming or post-assembly validation is safer.
[16:30] Tom Reyes: We tried streaming and hit partial JSON issues. We'll switch to non-stream for parsing-critical routes.
[16:45] Maya Chen: I'll note that. Also, for token efficiency, try prefix caching when users have repeated prefixes. It reduces cost and latency.
[17:00] Tom Reyes: Are there client-side helpers for caching?
[17:04] Liam O'Connor: We have patterns — we'll include a lightweight cache example in the repo.
[17:20] Priya Mehta: Anything on rollout strategies? We want canary only on 5% traffic initially.
[17:28] Maya Chen: Console supports canary percentages, rollback, and automatic fallback to previous model variant. We'll configure that once you spin up Dedicated or a pinned hosted variant.
[17:45] Tom Reyes: For the shared artifacts, please put the demo repo, SDK snippet, and security pack in the shared drive link.
[17:52] Maya Chen: Will do.
[18:10] Jorge Alvarez: One last question — do you retain the raw customer payloads? We need clarity for retention and legal.
[18:20] Maya Chen: For hosted we retain request/response by default but can set redaction and retention policies; Dedicated/Private gives you full control. I'll have the security doc with the exact policy text.
[18:40] Tom Reyes: Ok, timeline recap — we'll run the 1k integration, try structured_output with strict stops, send the failure samples, and reconvene next week.
[19:00] Maya Chen: Recap of action items — Maya send SDK snippet + repo, Liam send Node examples and notes on sequence/parallel, Tom run integration and paste logs, Jorge send compliance Qs. Next meeting 2026-03-25 same time tentative.
[19:20] Priya Mehta: Thanks everyone.
[19:25] Aisha Khan: Thanks.
[19:30] Meeting ends.

Shared artifacts referenced: https://redwood.example.com/demo-repo (demo repo), https://redwood.example.com/security-pack (security docs), Shared sheet: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/brightpath-integration (results sheet).
